I'm Zainab, and I got into my dream college in Delhi last July. I'd wanted it since Class 9; its name was on a sticky note above my desk for four years. When the result came, Ammi cried, Abbu gave sweets to the whole lane, and I felt like I was flying.
By October, I felt like I'd landed in an empty field. Classes were fine. Aditi, my roommate, was lovely. The campus was everything I'd pictured. And yet I'd wake up and lie there thinking, now what? For four years every morning had a reason: one more chapter, one more mock test. Now the reason was gone and nothing had replaced it. I wasn't sad, just quietly tired in a strange way.
One night Aditi asked why I kept staring at the ceiling. I said, "I think I miss wanting something." Saying it out loud helped a little. I'm still looking for the next thing to want.

Mentor's note, first-year engineering. Harish Nair, faculty mentor.
Ojas (18) came to our monthly check-in today. He chose this college as his first choice after years of preparation; his family held a small function when he got in. On paper he is fine: full attendance, average marks.
But he looked flat. When I asked what he enjoys here, he shrugged. "Sir, for three years I knew exactly what I was doing every day. Now I've got it, and nothing is pulling me." He said he sleeps till the last minute, not because he is tired, but because there's no reason to get up early.
He isn't in crisis, but I don't want to leave this. I've invited him to the robotics club's open evening on Friday and asked a second-year, Kunal, to walk him there. We'll meet again in two weeks, and I've told him the student counsellor's door is open if the flatness grows.

Tuesday night, three weeks into college
I'm here. I made it. The design college I've wanted since Class 8. The one I cried about when the list came out.
So why do I feel like this?
Every morning I walk past the gate with the big letters, and I wait for the happy feeling to come back. It doesn't. The classes are fine. People are nice. I just feel hollow, like someone took out the engine and left the car.
Eshaan called today and asked if I'm loving it. I said yes. I didn't know how to explain that for four years I always knew what to do next. Practise. Portfolio. Entrance. And now there's no next.
Maybe I need a new "next". A smaller one.
– Vidya

Tushar looked at the bench where he used to study and felt something like homesickness for his old hunger.
